questions.question: What is an Amazon Machine Image (AMI)?

options.text: A physical server in AWS data center
A pre-configured template for launching EC2 instances
A backup of your AWS account
A monitoring tool for EC2 instances

explanation.correct: An AMI is a template that contains the operating system, applications, files, and configuration settings needed to launch EC2 instances. It acts as a blueprint for creating virtual servers.
explanation.why: Option A is incorrect because AMIs are software templates, not physical hardware. Option C describes AWS Backup or snapshots, not AMIs. Option D describes CloudWatch, not AMIs. AMIs specifically provide the software configuration for instances.

questions.question: Which AMI type offers the highest level of trust and regular security updates from AWS?

options.text: Community AMIs
Marketplace AMIs
Official AWS AMIs
Third-party AMIs

explanation.correct: Official AWS AMIs are created and maintained by Amazon, providing the highest trust level with regular security patches and updates directly from AWS.
explanation.why: Community AMIs (A) are unverified and created by random users. Marketplace AMIs (B) come from vendors but aren't AWS-maintained. Third-party AMIs (D) are from external vendors without AWS verification. Only Official AMIs receive direct AWS maintenance and updates.

questions.question: What are the four essential components contained in every AMI?

options.text: CPU, RAM, Storage, Network
Operating System, Applications, Files, Configuration Settings
Region, Availability Zone, VPC, Subnet
Instance Type, Key Pair, Security Group, AMI

explanation.correct: Every AMI contains four components: Operating System (base OS), Applications (pre-installed software), Files (configuration files and data), and Configuration Settings (system parameters).
explanation.why: Option A describes hardware components, not AMI contents. Option C lists AWS infrastructure elements, not AMI components. Option D lists EC2 launch requirements, not AMI contents. AMIs are purely software templates.

questions.question: If you create an AMI in the us-east-1 region, where is it available by default?

options.text: All AWS regions globally
Only in us-east-1 region
All regions in the United States
Automatically copied to us-west-1 and us-west-2

explanation.correct: AMIs are region-specific resources. An AMI created in us-east-1 is only available in that region unless you explicitly copy it to other regions.
explanation.why: AMIs don't automatically replicate globally (A), across US regions (C), or to specific regions (D). This regional isolation ensures data residency compliance and gives you control over where your templates exist.

questions.question: What is the primary risk of using Community AMIs in production environments?

options.text: They are too expensive
They are completely unverified and may contain malware or backdoors
They only work in specific regions
They require special AWS permissions

explanation.correct: Community AMIs are created by anyone with an AWS account and receive zero verification from AWS. They could contain malware, backdoors, vulnerable software, or cryptocurrency miners.
explanation.why: Community AMIs are free (A is wrong). They work in any region they're shared to (C is wrong). They don't require special permissions (D is wrong). The real danger is their completely unvetted nature - never use them for production.

questions.question: What is the relationship between an AMI and an EC2 instance?

options.text: They are the same thing with different names
AMI is the running server, instance is the template
AMI is the template, EC2 instance is the running server created from that template
AMI stores data, EC2 instance processes data

explanation.correct: An AMI is a static template/blueprint, while an EC2 instance is the live, running virtual machine created from that AMI. One AMI can create unlimited instances.
explanation.why: They're not the same (A). The relationship isn't reversed - AMI is always the template, not the running server (B). Their purpose isn't data storage vs processing (D). Think of it like a house blueprint (AMI) versus actual houses built from that blueprint (instances).

questions.question: Approximately what percentage of cloud instances run Linux rather than Windows?

explanation.correct: Approximately 70% of all EC2 instances run Linux distributions, while only 30% run Windows. This is due to Linux's zero licensing costs, lower resource requirements, and superior automation capabilities.
explanation.why: Linux significantly dominates cloud computing (not 30% or 50%). While Linux is very popular, it's not quite 90% - Windows still holds about 30% for .NET applications and Windows-specific workloads.

questions.question: Which port is used for SSH connections to Linux instances?

options.text: Port 80
Port 443
Port 22
Port 3389

explanation.correct: SSH (Secure Shell) uses port 22 for secure remote access to Linux and Unix systems. This is the standard port for command-line access to Linux instances.
explanation.why: Port 80 is HTTP (A), port 443 is HTTPS (B), and port 3389 is RDP for Windows (D). Port 22 is specifically reserved for SSH protocol and must be allowed in Security Groups to access Linux instances remotely.

questions.question: Which Linux component is responsible for managing hardware resources like CPU, memory, and disk?

options.text: The Shell
GNU Utilities
The Linux Kernel
User Applications

explanation.correct: The Linux kernel is the core of the operating system that directly manages all hardware resources including process scheduling, memory allocation, device drivers, and file systems.
explanation.why: The Shell (A) is just the command interpreter. GNU Utilities (B) are command-line tools. User Applications (D) run on top of the kernel. Only the kernel has direct hardware access and resource management responsibility.

questions.question: What does CLI stand for and why is it important in cloud computing?

options.text: Cloud Linux Interface - required for EC2
Command Line Interface - enables automation and scripting
Central Login Interface - for AWS Console access
Compute Level Integration - for instance management

explanation.correct: CLI stands for Command Line Interface, which is crucial in cloud computing because it enables automation, scripting, Infrastructure as Code, and remote management via text commands.
explanation.why: CLI is not Cloud Linux Interface (A), Central Login Interface (C), or Compute Level Integration (D). The command-line interface allows DevOps teams to automate infrastructure management, which would be impossible with only graphical interfaces.

questions.question: Which command would you use to view the last 10 lines of a log file and continue watching new lines as they're added?

options.text: cat logfile.txt
head -10 logfile.txt
tail -f logfile.txt
grep logfile.txt

explanation.correct: The 'tail -f' command shows the last lines of a file and follows it in real-time, displaying new lines as they're written. This is essential for monitoring live application logs.
explanation.why: cat (A) shows entire file but doesn't follow updates. head (B) shows first lines, not last. grep (D) searches for patterns but doesn't follow files. tail -f is specifically designed for monitoring log files in real-time.

questions.question: What does the 'chmod 400 mykey.pem' command do?

options.text: Changes the file size to 400 bytes
Sets the file to read-only for owner, no access for others
Deletes the file after 400 seconds
Creates 400 copies of the file

explanation.correct: chmod 400 sets file permissions to read-only for the owner (4 = read) and no permissions for group or others (00). This is required for SSH private key files for security.
explanation.why: chmod doesn't change file size (A), set deletion timers (C), or create copies (D). The 400 in chmod represents permission bits: 4 (read) for owner, 0 (no access) for group, 0 (no access) for others.

questions.question: When you stop an EC2 instance (not terminate), what happens to the data on attached EBS volumes?

options.text: All data is permanently deleted
Data is preserved and you're charged for EBS storage
Data is automatically backed up to S3
Data is moved to Instance Store

explanation.correct: When you stop an instance, EBS volumes remain attached and all data is preserved. You stop paying for instance compute charges but continue paying for EBS storage (typically much cheaper).
explanation.why: Data isn't deleted when stopped - only when terminated with delete-on-termination enabled (A is wrong). Stopping doesn't trigger S3 backups (C). Instance Store would actually be lost on stop, EBS persists (D is wrong). This is a key cost optimization strategy.

questions.question: Your company needs to launch 100 web servers with identical configuration. What's the most efficient approach?

options.text: Manually configure each server one by one
Create a custom AMI from one configured server, then launch 100 instances from it
Use Community AMIs for quick setup
Launch 100 instances and use a configuration script on each

explanation.correct: Creating a custom AMI from one perfectly configured server allows you to launch 100 identical instances in minutes. This ensures consistency and saves enormous time compared to repeated configuration.
explanation.why: Manual configuration (A) would take days and risk inconsistencies. Community AMIs (C) are security risks. While configuration scripts (D) work, they're slower than AMIs and can fail mid-execution. Custom AMIs are the professional standard for rapid, consistent scaling.

questions.question: What are Security Groups in EC2, and what is their key characteristic?

options.text: IAM groups that control AWS Console access
Stateful virtual firewalls that control inbound and outbound traffic
Physical security in AWS data centers
Backup groups for disaster recovery

explanation.correct: Security Groups are stateful virtual firewalls that control network traffic to instances. Stateful means if you allow inbound traffic, the response is automatically allowed outbound.
explanation.why: Security Groups aren't IAM groups (A), physical security (C), or backup systems (D). They're instance-level firewalls. The stateful nature is crucial: you only need inbound rules for incoming connections; return traffic is automatically permitted.

questions.question: Which Linux distribution is specifically optimized for AWS and includes no licensing costs?

options.text: Red Hat Enterprise Linux
Windows Server
Amazon Linux 2023
macOS Server

explanation.correct: Amazon Linux 2023 is AWS's own Linux distribution, optimized for EC2, completely free, and includes AWS-specific optimizations and integrations.
explanation.why: RHEL (A) requires paid subscriptions. Windows Server (B) has licensing fees and isn't Linux. macOS (D) isn't available on EC2. Amazon Linux 2023 is purpose-built for AWS, free, and receives long-term support from AWS.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a Key Pair in EC2, and what happens if you lose the private key?

options.text: It encrypts data at rest; AWS can recover lost keys
It enables SSH authentication; lost keys cannot be recovered and you lose access
It's used for billing; you can request a new one from support
It controls instance start/stop; it's not critical for access

explanation.correct: Key Pairs use public-key cryptography for SSH authentication. The private key proves you're authorized to access the instance. If lost, there's no recovery - you permanently lose access to the instance.
explanation.why: Key pairs aren't for data encryption (A), billing (C), or instance control (D). They're solely for authentication. AWS cannot recover lost private keys because they're generated cryptographically and AWS never stores your private key.

questions.question: Which UNIX principle is most directly reflected in modern microservices architecture?

options.text: Use graphical interfaces for everything
Do one thing well and work together through standard interfaces
Always use the newest technology available
Build monolithic applications for simplicity

explanation.correct: The UNIX principle 'do one thing well' and 'programs work together' directly inspired microservices: each service handles one function and communicates via APIs, just like UNIX commands chain together via pipes.
explanation.why: UNIX emphasizes command-line (not GUI) (A), simplicity over novelty (C), and modularity over monoliths (D). The microservices pattern of single-responsibility services communicating through well-defined interfaces is pure UNIX philosophy applied to modern cloud architecture.

questions.question: What type of software testing would you use to verify that your web application can handle 10,000 concurrent users?

options.text: Unit Testing
Integration Testing
Performance Testing (Load/Stress Testing)
Security Testing

explanation.correct: Performance testing, specifically load testing and stress testing, measures how systems behave under various user loads. This identifies bottlenecks and capacity limits before production deployment.
explanation.why: Unit testing (A) tests individual code functions. Integration testing (B) verifies components work together. Security testing (D) finds vulnerabilities. Only performance testing simulates high user loads to validate scalability and identify breaking points.

questions.question: In the Linux layered architecture, which layer sits directly between the kernel and user applications?

options.text: Hardware
System Libraries and GNU Utilities
Network Stack
Device Drivers

explanation.correct: System libraries and GNU utilities sit between the kernel and applications, providing reusable code functions and command-line tools that applications use to interact with the kernel.
explanation.why: Hardware (A) is below the kernel. Network Stack and Device Drivers (C, D) are part of the kernel itself. System libraries provide the interface between applications and kernel, handling system calls and providing common functions.

questions.question: Your production EC2 instance is running critical services. What's the difference between rebooting and stopping/starting the instance?

options.text: No difference - both restart the instance the same way
Reboot keeps same host hardware and IP; Stop/Start may change host and public IP
Reboot deletes data; Stop/Start preserves data
Stop/Start is faster than reboot

explanation.correct: Reboot restarts the OS on the same physical host, keeping public IP addresses. Stop/Start may migrate the instance to different hardware and assign a new public IP (private IP and Elastic IP persist).
explanation.why: They're not the same (A). Neither deletes EBS data (C). Reboot is actually faster than Stop/Start (D). The key difference is host persistence: reboot stays on same hardware, stop/start may migrate, which affects IP addresses and is important for disaster recovery planning.

questions.question: What does the Linux command 'ps aux | grep nginx' accomplish?

options.text: Installs nginx web server
Lists all processes, then filters to show only nginx-related processes
Stops the nginx service
Shows nginx error logs

explanation.correct: 'ps aux' lists all running processes. The pipe '|' sends that output to 'grep nginx', which filters to show only lines containing 'nginx'. This is a common way to check if a service is running.
explanation.why: This doesn't install software (A), stop services (C), or show logs (D). It demonstrates UNIX pipe philosophy: chaining simple commands together. 'ps' does one thing (list processes), 'grep' does one thing (filter text), together they solve the problem.

questions.question: Which EC2 instance state incurs full compute charges?

options.text: Pending
Stopped
Running
Terminated

explanation.correct: Only the Running state incurs full compute charges (per-hour or per-second billing). This includes CPU, memory, and network bandwidth costs.
explanation.why: Pending (A) doesn't charge - AWS is allocating resources. Stopped (B) only charges for EBS storage. Terminated (D) has no charges. Understanding this is critical for cost management: stop instances when not in use to save 70-90% on costs.

questions.question: Why is command-line interface (CLI) preferred over graphical interface (GUI) for managing large cloud infrastructures?

options.text: CLI looks more professional
CLI enables automation, scripting, and managing hundreds of servers simultaneously
GUI is not available in AWS
CLI is easier for beginners

explanation.correct: CLI enables Infrastructure as Code, automation scripts, and batch operations across hundreds of servers. You can write one script to configure 1000 servers instead of clicking through GUI 1000 times.
explanation.why: It's not about looking professional (A). AWS has a GUI Console (C). CLI is actually harder initially for beginners (D). The real power is automation: DevOps practices, CI/CD pipelines, configuration management - all rely on command-line tools that can be scripted and version-controlled.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of creating custom AMIs in a production environment?

options.text: To save money on AWS bills
To ensure rapid, consistent deployment with all software pre-configured
To comply with AWS Terms of Service
To enable EC2 instances to run

explanation.correct: Custom AMIs enable infrastructure standardization and rapid scaling. By pre-configuring one perfect server and saving it as an AMI, you can launch hundreds of identical, production-ready servers in minutes.
explanation.why: Custom AMIs don't directly save money - stopped instances do (A). They're not required by AWS ToS (C) or to run instances (D). The real value is operational: ensuring every server is identically configured, reducing deployment time from hours to minutes, and eliminating configuration drift between environments.

questions.question: Your company deploys updates weekly and needs to maintain the ability to rollback. How should you structure your AMI strategy?

options.text: Use the same AMI indefinitely and apply updates via scripts
Create a new AMI after each deployment with version numbers and dates, retain last 3-5 versions
Only create AMIs annually
Use Community AMIs for the latest updates

explanation.correct: Create versioned AMIs after each significant deployment (e.g., WebServer-v2.3-20251006), retaining recent versions. This enables instant rollback to known-good configurations if new deployments fail.
explanation.why: Never updating the AMI (A) defeats the purpose and causes configuration drift. Annual AMIs (C) are too infrequent. Community AMIs (D) are security risks. Version-controlled AMIs provide deployment history and instant rollback capability - critical for production stability.

questions.question: In a multi-tier application (web, app, database), how should AMIs be organized?

options.text: One AMI containing all tiers
Separate AMIs for each tier (web-server AMI, app-server AMI, database AMI)
No AMIs needed, configure each instance manually
Use different AMIs for each developer

explanation.correct: Create separate AMIs for each tier. Each tier has different software, configurations, and scaling needs. This allows independent scaling and updating of each tier.
explanation.why: One monolithic AMI (A) prevents independent scaling and updates. Manual configuration (C) is error-prone and slow. Per-developer AMIs (D) create management nightmares. Separate tier AMIs follow single-responsibility principle and enable independent lifecycle management.

questions.question: What is the relationship between instance type and AMI when launching an EC2 instance?

options.text: AMI determines hardware, instance type determines software
They are mutually exclusive - choose one or the other
AMI determines software configuration, instance type determines hardware specifications
Instance type must match the AMI's recommended size

explanation.correct: AMI defines WHAT runs on the server (OS, applications, configuration). Instance type defines HOW POWERFUL the server is (CPU, RAM, network). They're independent: same AMI can run on t3.micro or m5.24xlarge.
explanation.why: The relationship isn't reversed (A). They're not mutually exclusive - you need both (B). There's no requirement to match sizes (D). This separation allows flexible scaling: use same AMI (software) with different instance types (hardware) based on workload needs.

questions.question: How do the Linux kernel's process management and memory management functions relate to EC2 instance performance?

options.text: They don't affect EC2 - AWS manages everything
The kernel allocates CPU time and RAM to applications, directly impacting instance responsiveness
Only AWS hypervisor matters, not the guest kernel
These functions only matter for bare metal instances

explanation.correct: The Linux kernel inside your instance manages process scheduling (which apps get CPU when) and memory allocation. Poor kernel configuration or resource exhaustion causes slow performance even on large instance types.
explanation.why: AWS manages the hypervisor, but your kernel manages resources within your instance (A is wrong). The guest kernel absolutely matters for performance (C is wrong). This applies to all instance types, not just bare metal (D). Understanding kernel resource management is essential for performance troubleshooting.

questions.question: Why would a DevOps team implement automated AMI creation as part of their CI/CD pipeline?

options.text: To comply with AWS licensing requirements
To create immutable infrastructure where each deployment produces a new versioned AMI
Because manual AMI creation is not possible
To reduce the number of EC2 instances needed

explanation.correct: Automated AMI creation supports immutable infrastructure practices: each successful build creates a new AMI version. Deployments launch instances from new AMIs rather than updating existing instances, enabling instant rollback and eliminating configuration drift.
explanation.why: No licensing requirement exists (A). Manual AMI creation is possible but doesn't scale (C). AMI automation doesn't reduce instance count (D). The pattern is: code commit → build → test → create AMI → deploy from AMI. This ensures every production instance matches tested artifacts exactly.
